summary: To stop people from impersonating telephone numbers, there must be a way to prove who has authority over a number. This document describes how X.509 certificates can be used for that purpose, as one part of the broader STIR architecture for authenticated calling.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8226 defines how certificates can support claims that a caller is authorized to use a telephone number. A verifier checks the certificate and the number-authority information before relying on the caller's signed identity.

subtitle: How X.509 certificates can assert which telephone numbers a caller is authorized to use.

tldr.problem: A caller can present a telephone number that is not assigned to them, and a verifier needs a way to check whether the signer is authorized to use that number.
tldr.mechanism: An X.509 certificate can show authority through its subject or through a TN Authorization List extension containing service-provider codes, number ranges or individual numbers. A separate extension can constrain claims in a PASSporT.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies credential formats and verification requirements for the STIR architecture, while leaving certificate freshness choices for further study. RFC 8226 is updated by RFC 9118.

facts.label: Required signature algorithms
facts.value: ECDSA P-256 and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5

today: RFC 8226 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9118. It defines the certificate credential formats used with the STIR architecture.

sections.title: Telephone Numbers as Verified Identities
sections.content:
Impersonating a calling number can support robocalling, vishing and other attacks. A credential system can help a caller show that an authority has approved its use of a telephone number. This RFC describes that system using X.509 version 3 certificates.

The specification is written for the Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR) architecture, where an authentication service signs and a verification service checks a call identity. It defines certificate syntax and meaning, but does not require a particular certification authority or deployment model.
sections.plainLanguage: A caller's number needs more than a text label to show who may use it. Certificates let an authority make a verifiable statement about that permission.

sections.title: Two Ways to Establish Number Authority
sections.content:
The first approach uses the certificate subject, such as a carrier's domain name or a Service Provider Code. The verifier decides whether that subject is authorized for the number by using an external data source or a trust relationship.

The second approach places the scope directly in a TN Authorization List extension. The list can name telephone numbers, number ranges or provider codes, and it may appear in the certificate or be obtained from a network service. The approaches can be combined. The STIR signing format remains the same; the verifier's authorization decision changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A verifier can rely on who the certificate names, or check a list of telephone numbers covered by the certificate. Either method supports the same call-signing format.

sections.title: Certificate Algorithms and Retrieval
sections.content:
Implementations must support ECDSA with the P-256 curve and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 for certificate signatures. RSA support is described as transitional because it is already widely used in public-key infrastructures. Certificates must also provide key material for ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256, used for the ES256 signatures required by PASSporT.

Verifiers can receive a certificate with the SIP request or retrieve it from the URI in the Identity header's info parameter. Implementations must support the CID, SIP and HTTP URI schemes and must support SIP, HTTP and HTTPS retrieval as specified. The verifier must trust the certificate's trust anchor and determine whether the certificate is fresh.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates use required signature algorithms and can be delivered with a call or fetched by URI. A verifier still has to trust the issuer and check whether the certificate remains current.

sections.title: Enrollment, Authorization and Delegation
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to enroll a number holder. A certification authority may work with numbering authorities and carriers; it may require an applicant to prove control of the number, such as through a test; or a certificate holder may delegate some or all of its authority to another party.

Delegation can have multiple levels, but long chains can be fragile and slow verification. The private key is held by the entity that signs calls; the RFC recommends distributing private-key material in PKCS #8 objects signed by a trusted entity.
sections.plainLanguage: An authority can issue a certificate through the number-assignment chain, a proof-of-control process, or delegation from an existing holder. Long delegation chains can make checking a call slower and less reliable.

sections.title: Number Lists and Claim Limits
sections.content:
The TN Authorization List extension identifies one or more authorized number entries. An entry can be a Service Provider Code, a range with a starting number and count, or one telephone number. A telephone number is an IA5String of 1 to 15 characters from digits, hash and asterisk. Range counts cannot make the resulting number longer than its starting number.

A separate optional JWT Claim Constraints extension lets an issuer require named PASSporT claims or restrict a claim to listed values. It applies constraints to what an authentication service may sign, and a verifier checks those constraints.

For large number holdings, the authorization list may be provided by reference using an Authority Information Access extension. Its id-ad-stirTNList method points to an HTTPS URI that returns the complete DER-encoded list with media type application/tnauthlist.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate can cover a provider code, a range of numbers or one number. It can also limit which claims a signer may include in the signed call identity.

sections.title: Freshness and Revocation
sections.content:
Number assignments can change, for example through number portability. A verifier must therefore check both that the certificate is valid and that the signer still has authority for the telephone number being checked. The RFC describes two options: short-lived certificates without a status check, or status information from the authority such as OCSP.

The document makes no recommendation between these options. It says that certificate freshness needs more study and implementation experience. Checking status online may reveal private information, and future freshness mechanisms must explain those risks and possible countermeasures.
sections.plainLanguage: Telephone numbers can change owners, so a valid certificate may no longer cover the number. Verifiers need a way to check current authority, but this RFC does not choose one freshness method.

sections.title: Privacy and Certificate Security
sections.content:
A certificate or referenced list can reveal telephone numbers unrelated to the call under review. A Service Provider Code can also connect a certificate to a carrier and, with industry databases, to its numbers. Short-lived certificates for individual numbers are one approach the RFC discusses for limiting those links.

A referenced list is returned over HTTPS, which protects it in transit, but the list is not a signed object. The verifier therefore trusts the server to return the list faithfully. The RFC points to the ordinary certificate-security practices in RFC 5280.
sections.plainLanguage: A list covering many numbers can expose information that a call verifier does not need. HTTPS protects a downloaded list while it travels, but the verifier must trust the server that supplies it.
